title: You Can Add Thousands of Online Friends, Yet Your Brain Caps Real Ties Near One Fifty
description:
Experimental Chronicle — Robin Dunbar (1992-1995): Primate Neocortex Ratio & the ~150 Social-Group Limit, grounded in R.I.M. Dunbar (1992) (Journal of Human Evolution). Empirical findings show that why do primates carry such metabolically expensive, oversized brains (~20% of resting human energy for 2% of body mass)? In 1992, UCL anthropologist Robin Dunbar tested ecological foraging theories (fruit-map range size) head-to-head against the 'Social Brain Hypothesis' across 38 primate genera.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how prefrontal cortex, temporal lobe coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that territory size and diet failed to explain neocortex expansion cleanly — instead, mean SOCIAL GROUP SIZE correlated remarkably strongly (r^2 ~ 0.60-0.76) with the neocortex ratio (neocortex volume divided by the rest of the brain).

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- R.I.M. Dunbar (1992). Neocortex size as a constraint on group size in primates. Journal of Human Evolution. https://doi.org/10.1016/0047-2484(92)90081-j
- R.I.M. Dunbar (1995). Neocortex size and group size in primates: a test of the hypothesis. Journal of Human Evolution. https://doi.org/10.1006/jhev.1995.1021
- R. A. Hill, R. I. M. Dunbar (2003). Social network size in humans. Human Nature. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12110-003-1016-y

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
